source.title: AfriqueLLM: How Data Mixing and Model Architecture Impact Continued Pre-training for African Languages
source.authors: Hao Yu; Tian-Yi Xu; Michael A. Hedderich; W. Hamidouche; Syed Waqas Zamir; David Ifeoluwa Adelani

record.tranche_reason: Reports downstream benchmark scores across model sizes and model families, a different measure from the pretraining-loss scaling laws; it does not fit or test power laws in held-out loss.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior scaling laws and calls its within-architecture size result consistent with them. The reported final training losses in Table 13 are not held-out losses and are not a scale sweep with other factors controlled, so they do not test V1–V3. Rows below record the paper's reported aggregate downstream scores across size, relevant to V6; the paper does not report fitted curves or prediction errors.
record.test_reason: The study gives no loss curves or fits. It does report downstream AfroBench-Lite scores for 2–3 sizes within the Gemma 3 and Qwen 3 families, before and after continued pre-training (CPT). That bears weakly on V6 (downstream performance improving with scale) in a new setting: African-language CPT. The sizes are off-the-shelf checkpoints whose pretraining tokens are not controlled, so this is a coarse check of direction, not of predictability.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Within a fixed architecture larger models generally perform better, but across families scale alone is not predictive and architecture and data dominate. The main conclusion is that the CPT data mixture is the primary driver of gains.
record.recipe_differences: The study performs continued pre-training and downstream benchmark evaluation; it does not use the original loss-scaling-law fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported downstream scores vary with model family/architecture and size; CPT data mixture also affects task outcomes, though the rows here cover the CMS size comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: Relative CPT gain does not shrink consistently with size. Gemma: +18.8% (4B) vs +7.3% (12B). Qwen: +74.4%, +76.5%, +57.8% (4B/8B/14B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of continued pre-training decreases with base-model size within a family.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The size comparisons cover only a few sizes (Gemma 3: 4B and 12B; Qwen 3: 4B, 8B and 14B; Llama 3.1: 8B only), with architecture varying across families. Reported outcomes are aggregate downstream benchmark scores, not held-out loss or predictions from fitted scaling curves. No uncertainty estimates are reported for these aggregate scores.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained. Tables 2 and 7 compare data mixtures or training variants at fixed size rather than testing downstream scaling with model size; Table 13 reports final training loss, not held-out loss.

untested.parts: All: no held-out loss scaling. Table 13 reports final training loss across different architectures.
All: no shape sweep at fixed parameter count.
All: no power-law fits for CPT or other regimes.
Predictability in the quantitative sense: no fitted curves, prediction errors, or loss-to-downstream mapping. Sizes are off-the-shelf checkpoints with uncontrolled pretraining data.

missing.what: Gemma 3 27B base aggregate score of 60.71, a third Gemma size continuing the within-family rise. The authors also note AfriqueQwen-14B beats it at under half the size.
Per-task within-family scores showing non-monotonic cases, e.g. Qwen 3 SIB-200 57.88 (4B) vs 53.06 (8B)

record.verdict_notes: This is weak evidence for V6: 2–3 off-the-shelf sizes per family, with no control of pretraining tokens, no uncertainty estimates and no fits. The reader's 'partial' states were changed to 'observed' because the within-family rises are monotonic. The paper's mention of 'scaling laws' refers to cited work.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss across parameters, tokens, or compute; bottleneck conditions and power-law fits.
Prediction of larger-run held-out loss from fits to smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Held-out loss comparisons controlling parameter count while varying depth, width, or other architecture details.
Power-law loss in other modalities or training regimes.
Prediction from pretraining loss, fitted scaling curves, and systematic prediction accuracy; the paper reports aggregate downstream scores by model size, not these.
Sensitivity of fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal allocation to setup and fitting choices.

relationships.condition: Within family (Gemma 3 4B/12B, Qwen 3 4B/8B/14B), base and CMS-adapted aggregate AfroBench-Lite scores
relationships.reason: Aggregate scores rise monotonically with size in both families, before and after CPT (r2–r6, r8–r12). No fitted curve is given.
relationships.display_finding: Aggregate AfroBench-Lite scores increased monotonically with size in both families before and after continued pretraining, without a fitted scaling curve.

relationships.condition: Across model families, and per individual task
relationships.reason: Size does not order scores across families. Base Gemma 3 4B (40.31) beats Qwen 3 8B (33.47). Adapted AfriqueQwen-8B (59.08) beats AfriqueGemma-12B (58.82). Some per-task results are non-monotonic, e.g. base Qwen SIB-200 at 8B < 4B (r1–r12).
relationships.display_finding: Gemma 3 4B beat Qwen 3 8B (40.31 versus 33.47), AfriqueQwen-8B beat AfriqueGemma-12B (59.08 versus 58.82), and base Qwen 8B underperformed 4B on SIB-200.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Within the reported Gemma 3 and Qwen 3 families, for base and CMS-adapted aggregate AfroBench-Lite scores
reader_labels.reason: Aggregate scores rise with size in both reported within-family comparisons: Gemma 3 4B to 12B (r2–r3; adapted r8–r9) and Qwen 3 4B to 8B to 14B (r4–r6; adapted r10–r12). The study does not establish a fitted or predictive scaling curve.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Comparisons across model families at different parameter counts, and the single-size Llama result
reader_labels.reason: The paper says architectural choices dominate scale across families; its cross-family scores are not a single predictable size trend, and Llama has only one reported size (r1–r12).
